stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a non-healing ulcer on the lateral border of the tongue for 4 weeks. He has a 30-year history of smoking. The lesion is indurated and firm on palpation. There are no signs of acute infection or systemic illness. Oral examination suggests a high suspicion for oral squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

keywordsHtml:
1. Non-healing ulcer >4 weeks → red flag duration strongly suggests malignancy (oral SCC until proven otherwise).
  2. Indurated firm lesion on lateral tongue → classic feature of invasive epithelial malignancy.
  3. 30-year smoking history → major risk factor for oral squamous cell carcinoma, increases pre-test probability.

E.title: Incisional biopsy of the lesion
E.body: An incisional biopsy is the Gold Standard diagnostic procedure for suspected oral squamous cell carcinoma, especially when lesions are large or suspicious. It involves sampling a representative portion of the lesion, typically from the edge where normal and abnormal tissue meet, to preserve tissue architecture. This allows histopathological confirmation of malignancy and grading. It is essential before staging and treatment planning.
E.bodyHtml: An incisional biopsy is the Gold Standard diagnostic procedure for suspected oral squamous cell carcinoma, especially when lesions are large or suspicious. It involves sampling a representative portion of the lesion, typically from the edge where normal and abnormal tissue meet, to preserve tissue architecture. This allows histopathological confirmation of malignancy and grading. It is essential before staging and treatment planning.
E.clinicalReasoning: In this patient, the lesion is clinically malignant until proven otherwise due to duration, induration, and smoking history. The goal is to obtain a definitive tissue diagnosis. Incisional biopsy provides adequate depth and architecture, which is required to confirm invasion. It avoids complete excision of a potentially large malignant lesion and ensures proper oncologic planning.

A.title: Brush (exfoliative) cytology of the lesion
A.body: Brush cytology is a non-invasive screening method that collects superficial epithelial cells from mucosal surfaces. It is mainly used for initial evaluation of oral lesions but does not preserve tissue architecture. Therefore, it cannot determine invasion, which is essential for diagnosing carcinoma. It may help detect dysplasia but is not confirmatory.
A.bodyHtml: Brush cytology is a non-invasive screening method that collects superficial epithelial cells from mucosal surfaces. It is mainly used for initial evaluation of oral lesions but does not preserve tissue architecture. Therefore, it cannot determine invasion, which is essential for diagnosing carcinoma. It may help detect dysplasia but is not confirmatory.
A.clinicalReasoning: Useful for screening suspicious lesions in low-resource settings. However, its inability to assess stromal invasion makes it unreliable for diagnosing OSCC. False negatives are common in keratinized or deeply invasive lesions. Hence, it cannot replace biopsy in high-risk patients.

B.title: Punch biopsy from the edge of the ulcer
B.body: Punch biopsy obtains a cylindrical tissue sample and may be used in accessible mucosal lesions. However, in oral cavity malignancy, it may not capture sufficient depth or representative invasive tissue. There is also a risk of sampling error if the lesion is heterogeneous. It is less preferred compared to incisional biopsy for oral SCC.
B.bodyHtml: Punch biopsy obtains a cylindrical tissue sample and may be used in accessible mucosal lesions. However, in oral cavity malignancy, it may not capture sufficient depth or representative invasive tissue. There is also a risk of sampling error if the lesion is heterogeneous. It is less preferred compared to incisional biopsy for oral SCC.
B.clinicalReasoning: While technically feasible, punch biopsy is not ideal for oral tongue lesions suspected of carcinoma. It may miss deeper invasive components and provide inadequate tissue architecture. Therefore, it is not the best initial diagnostic choice in high-risk malignant lesions.

C.title: Excisional biopsy of the lesion
C.body: Excisional biopsy involves complete removal of the lesion and is appropriate only for small, benign-appearing lesions. In suspected malignancy, complete excision without diagnosis is inappropriate because it interferes with staging and margin assessment. It may also lead to incomplete oncologic planning.

In suspected malignancy, complete excision without diagnosis is inappropriate because it interferes with staging and margin assessment. It may also lead to incomplete oncologic planning.
C.clinicalReasoning: In a lesion with high suspicion of malignancy, excisional biopsy risks inadequate oncologic margins and improper staging. It is contraindicated in large or suspicious oral lesions. Therefore, it is not recommended in this case.

D.title: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of adjacent cervical lymph node
D.body: FNAC is used to evaluate lymph node involvement in suspected malignancies. It is useful for staging confirmed cancers but does not diagnose the primary mucosal lesion. It cannot determine the histopathology of the tongue ulcer itself.
D.bodyHtml: FNAC is used to evaluate lymph node involvement in suspected malignancies. It is useful for staging confirmed cancers but does not diagnose the primary mucosal lesion. It cannot determine the histopathology of the tongue ulcer itself.
D.clinicalReasoning: This test is appropriate only if lymphadenopathy is present and malignancy is already confirmed. It plays a role in staging, not primary diagnosis. Therefore, it is not suitable as the initial diagnostic step here.

keyConcept: A chronic indurated oral ulcer in a smoker is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma, and the definitive diagnostic step is incisional biopsy for histopathological confirmation before any staging or treatment.

diagram.name: Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma – Diagnostic Approach to Chronic Non-Healing Tongue Ulcer
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the systematic diagnostic approach to a chronic non-healing tongue ulcer suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). It highlights key clinical red flags including persistent ulceration, induration, lateral tongue involvement, and tobacco exposure. The flowchart emphasizes the importance of thorough oral and cervical lymph node examination, followed by incisional biopsy as the gold standard for definitive diagnosis. Additional staging investigations such as contrast-enhanced imaging and FNAC of cervical lymph nodes are also demonstrated to assess local spread and metastasis.
